strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across three datasets (MACSumDial, MACSumDoc, DialogSum) and multiple model sizes (1B-70B), with impressive finding that 1B PACO matches 70B baseline performance

Novel problem formulation: reframing multi-attribute controllable summarization as sequential planning is well-motivated and intuitive, addressing a real limitation of LLMs attempting simultaneous constraint satisfaction
Training-free approach provides genuine flexibility and generalizability compared to fine-tuned baselines, making it practically applicable to new attributes without retraining
Thoughtful algorithmic design with summary-level nodes reducing search complexity, distinction between deterministic/non-deterministic attributes, and adaptive selection of only necessary attributes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with detailed ablations, multiple models/architectures, and thorough reproducibility information (hyperparameters, prompts, hardware specs)
Insightful analysis revealing that larger models control more sophisticated attributes (Figure 5) and that length has strong correlations with other attributes (Figure 6)
weaknesses: Severe practical limitation: 8.6× computational overhead (196s vs 23s per summary) compared to baseline severely limits real-world deployment; dismissed too quickly without exploring optimization strategies, pruning, or early stopping

Heuristic reward component is underdeveloped: ablation study (Table 4) shows minimal to negligible benefit (e.g., 1B Extractiveness: 9.30 vs 9.56), suggesting the value function design is incomplete despite claims of sophistication

Critical absence of human evaluation: no user studies validating that optimizing metrics (MAD, embedding similarity) translates to preferred summaries; ROUGE/BERTScore are known imperfect proxies, undermining claims about human-aligned summaries

Insufficient justification of key design choices: why maximize 'degree' over Q-value? Why reciprocal in Eq. 3? The reward function appears ad-hoc; hyperparameter sensitivity (α, β, ε) inadequately analyzed in main paper

Limited technical novelty in MCTS application: core algorithm components (PUCT, selection, expansion, evaluation, backpropagation) are standard; primary novelty is problem formulation and summary-level nodes rather than algorithmic innovation
Comparison fairness: HP+SP baseline trained on 406M BARTlarge versus contemporary 1B-70B models; retraining on same architectures would strengthen claims of superiority
No analysis of failure modes: when/why does PACO fail? Are certain attribute combinations incompatible? Missing qualitative error analysis and discussion of attributes most resistant to control
Scope limitations: only 5 attributes tested; scalability to many attributes unclear; all experiments on dialogue/document summarization with no evidence of generalization to other generation tasks
Statistical rigor issues: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or reported variance; single runs make small differences difficult to interpret as meaningful
PUCT formulation underspecified: connection between LLM's token probability π_θ(s,a) and attribute control actions unclear; how exactly does this prior inform exploration needs clarification

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of LLM limitations in simultaneous multi-attribute constraint satisfaction
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (MACSumDial, MACSumDoc, DialogSum) and multiple model sizes (1B, 7B, 70B), demonstrating robustness
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines, with notable gains on smaller models (e.g., 1B model length control: 55.68→17.96 MAD)
Reasonable design choice of summary-level nodes that reduces search complexity compared to token/sentence-level approaches
Thorough supplementary analyses including attribute frequency distribution, step-wise control patterns, ablation studies, and quality preservation metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore)
Strong reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, complete prompts in appendices, and explicit algorithms
weaknesses: Prohibitive computational cost: PACO requires 196.38s/summary vs. 22.83s baseline (8.6× slower), severely limiting practical applicability. Authors inadequately justify this trade-off, and appendix arguments about future efficiency improvements do not address current deployment constraints.

Limited technical novelty: MCTS for LLM generation is well-established (Yao et al. 2023, Hao et al. 2023, Wan et al. 2024). The primary contribution—summary-level nodes—is an incremental engineering optimization rather than a conceptual advance.

Heuristic reward component underperforms: Table 4 ablation shows combining local and heuristic rewards harms 1B model performance (length MAD: 17.96→21.98) and provides only marginal gains for 70B, questioning its value despite added complexity.
Absent human evaluation contradicts core claims: Abstract emphasizes 'alignment with user preferences' yet no human study validates controllability improvements or naturalness of refinements.

Narrow experimental scope: Limited to 5 binary attributes in single task (abstractive summarization); scalability to 10+ attributes unexplored; generalization to other constrained generation tasks unaddressed; generalizability across languages untested.

Questionable baseline comparisons: (a) HP+SP fine-tuned baseline underperforms despite being trained on task data—explanation via 'encoder-decoder structural constraints' is unsatisfying; (b) Self-planning baselines may be under-optimized; (c) Abstract's claim that 1B PACO 'rivals' 70B baseline conflates model size effects with method contribution.

Ad-hoc methodological choices lack justification: Degree-based final node selection (rather than highest-value) is unexplained; reciprocal reward normalization in Eq. 3 appears unprincipled; hyperparameter β=10 is sensitive (Table 5) but presented as universal.

Insufficient analysis of tree search efficiency: With max depth 5 and width 5 (3125 potential nodes), only 8 simulations per search explores a tiny fraction; convergence properties and exploration-exploitation trade-offs are unanalyzed.

Missing critical experiments: No scaling analysis for 10+ attributes; no oracle upper bounds; no cross-dataset generalization; no learned policy alternatives; no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters.
Statistical rigor gaps: No confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or variance analysis across multiple runs; stability of results unknown.

Limited investigation of attribute interdependencies: Paper mentions correlations but provides no systematic analysis of which attribute pairs conflict most or why MCTS-discovered orders differ across datasets (DialogSum specificity/length inversion unexplained).

Presentation issues: 'Training-free' is misleading (extensive inference required); heuristic score prompt (Appendix H) is task-specific and long—sensitivity to wording unexplored; some notation inconsistencies (a_t vs. a').

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Valid observation that LLMs struggle to simultaneously satisfy multiple correlated attribute constraints; sequential planning reframing is intuitive and well-justified
Training-free approach offers significant practical advantage: Enables flexibility and generalization compared to attribute-specific fine-tuning methods (MoE, hard/soft prompt tuning)
Strong and consistent empirical results: 1B PACO model achieves controllability comparable to 70B baseline; substantial improvements across all datasets/models (e.g., length MAD 55.68→17.96 on 1B)
Thoughtful technical design choices: Summary-level nodes reduce search complexity; deterministic vs. non-deterministic attribute distinction; adaptive selection via degree
Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple models (1B-70B), diverse datasets, thorough ablations, analysis of control patterns, fair baselines including self-planning variants
Maintains summary quality while improving controllability: ROUGE/BERTScore comparable to baselines, showing no quality-control tradeoff
Clear presentation: Excellent figures (especially Figure 3), detailed appendices with prompts and algorithms, honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead (~9x slower: 196s vs 22s per summary) substantially limits practical applicability; scalability concerns inadequately addressed; justification that higher cost is necessary for reasoning is circular
Missing human evaluation: No human assessment of controllability achievement, naturalness, quality tradeoffs; automatic metrics alone insufficient for claims about human-aligned summaries
Limited technical novelty: Primarily applies existing MCTS to summarization; main contributions (summary-level nodes, attribute type distinction) are incremental engineering choices

Incomplete analysis of attribute interactions: Motivates work with complex interdependencies but provides minimal systematic investigation; no analysis of conflicting attributes or failure modes; Figure 6 shows length dominates later steps but lacks deep analysis
Heuristic score ineffectiveness: Ablation study (Table 4) shows heuristic score provides minimal benefit, especially for 1B model; suggests underlying value function design weakness not addressed
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: Tree depth=5, simulations=8, α=1, β=10 appear somewhat arbitrary; no sensitivity analysis or search procedure described
Limited scope: Only 5 attributes tested; scalability to many attributes unclear; computational complexity grows combinatorially with attribute count
Attribute-specific engineering requirements: Adding new attributes requires custom reward functions and measurement code, somewhat contradicting flexibility claims
Limited baseline comparisons: Only one fine-tuned baseline (HP+SP, 406M); self-planning baselines are weak strawmen; missing recent multi-attribute control approaches
Dataset generalization concerns: Only 3 datasets in specific domains; DialogSum shows different patterns than MACSumDial/Doc, suggesting domain dependency; no out-of-domain evaluation
Reproducibility issues: Hyperparameters borrowed from Silver et al. 2017 without justification; no code release mentioned; undefined epsilon value and terminal condition thresholds
Insufficient ablations: No ablation on allowing all actions at all steps; decision rule (highest degree) not rigorously justified vs alternatives; no sensitivity to tree depth/simulations

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and addresses the real challenge of LLMs struggling with multiple correlated constraints simultaneously
Thoughtful technical design: summary-level nodes reduce search complexity; deterministic/non-deterministic attribute distinction; degree-based selection for adaptive control
Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple datasets, models of varying scales, proper baselines; remarkably shows 1B model matching 70B baseline performance
Training-free approach: eliminates need for attribute-specific fine-tuning, improving practical flexibility and generalization across attributes
Consistent improvements: outperforms baselines across all settings while preserving summary quality (ROUGE, BERTScore)
Good analysis: Figure 4 effectively demonstrates PACO produces more diverse control plans; ablation study on value function; interpretable frequency analysis
Reproducibility: detailed prompts, explicit hyperparameters, hardware specifications provided
weaknesses: Severe computational overhead: 8.6× slower than baseline (196s vs 23s per summary), significantly limiting practical deployment; dismissing this as acceptable for test-time inference is insufficient for high-volume applications
Scalability concerns: fixed to 5 attributes with max depth 5; no experiments or analysis on how method scales to 10+ attributes; unclear if computational cost becomes prohibitive
Heuristic value function provides negligible benefit (Table 4), raising questions about whether full MCTS formulation is necessary vs. simpler sequential refinement approaches

Incomplete attribute interaction analysis: identifies that attributes correlate (Fig. 6) but doesn't deeply investigate interdependencies or explain why certain orders are optimal; no analysis of failure modes

Evaluation methodology limitations: using reference summary targets is artificial (real users specify different targets); DialogSum discrepancy suggests dataset-dependent effectiveness not adequately explored; NER-based specificity metric is coarse

Ad-hoc design choices lacking principled justification: reciprocal formulation in Eq. 3, hyperparameters α=1 and β=10, undefined 'precisely controlled' terminal condition, unjustified max depth=5 and simulations=8; Table 5 shows β sensitivity suggesting these are tuning parameters
Limited novelty: MCTS application is straightforward adaptation; core contributions (summary-level nodes, adapted rewards) are incremental rather than conceptually novel
Stronger self-planning baselines not explored: Explicit self-planning+ underperforms despite adaptive prompting; alternative prompting strategies or reasoning techniques not investigated
Initial summary quality not analyzed: root node generation strategy could significantly affect performance but is not ablated; no robustness analysis for poor initializations
Missing comparisons: no greedy sequential baselines, beam search over control sequences, or reinforcement learning approaches; incomplete discussion of related tree-search methods for LLMs

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: LLMs struggle to enforce multiple correlated constraints simultaneously, and progressive refinement is intuitive
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets and multiple model sizes (1B, 7B, 70B) showing consistent improvements
Training-free approach avoiding expensive attribute-specific fine-tuning, providing practical flexibility
Thoughtful design choices: summary-level nodes reduce search complexity, deterministic/non-deterministic attribute distinction is sensible
Extensive reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and ablation studies
Clear presentation with informative figures effectively illustrating the approach
Consistent improvements over baselines across diverse settings and models
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applying existing MCTS to a new domain with straightforward customizations (summary-level nodes, attribute categorization). Similar MCTS applications to LLMs are increasingly common
Massive computational overhead not adequately justified: PACO requires ~196s vs. ~22s baseline (~9× slower). For practical deployment, this latency is problematic

Attribution concerns: budget-matched baselines (Random sequential achieves MAD 5.44 vs. PACO 4.91 on 70B) use similar computation yet remain competitive, suggesting gains may come from additional attempts rather than algorithmic superiority

Heuristic value function provides minimal benefit (Table 4): ablation shows heuristic score adds little, raising questions about MCTS's sophistication and whether the approach's complexity is justified
Weak self-planning baselines: LLM baselines perform surprisingly poorly, worse than baseline generation. Better prompts might substantially close the gap, undermining the core motivation for MCTS
Overstate claims: Abstract claims 1B PACO 'rivals' 70B baseline, but Table 1 shows 70B is still better on length (15.72 vs. 17.96 MAD). The claim should be more precise

Limited analysis of why MCTS matters: paper shows what happens (attribute frequencies, plan lengths) but not why MCTS's planning is necessary. No demonstration that structured search outweighs random ordering
No human evaluation: relying entirely on automatic metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore, MAD) for controllability assessment. Automatic metrics may not capture user satisfaction with attribute control
Beam search (beam=3) adds computation and introduces confound in fairness of comparison. Why not beam=1 for fairer baseline comparison?

Degree selection heuristic in decision stage (selecting highest-control node across tree) significantly deviates from standard MCTS without justification. This custom choice may drive performance gains
Limited scope: only English summarization tested; only 5 attributes; domain patterns differ (DialogSum vs. MACSum), raising generalization concerns; no comparison to constrained decoding
Ad-hoc hyperparameter balancing: β parameter for balancing attribute types requires tuning (Table 5 shows high sensitivity), no principled selection approach provided
Limited failure analysis: no discussion of which attribute combinations PACO struggles with or failure modes

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of why LLMs struggle with simultaneous multi-attribute constraints; progression to sequential planning is well-justified
Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple datasets (MACSumDial, MACSumDoc, DialogSum) and model scales (1B-70B), with 1B model achieving 3x improvement in length control over baseline

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thoughtful budget-matched baselines to isolate the value of structured planning, proper distinction between deterministic/non-deterministic attributes, and thorough ablations
Training-free approach offers significant practical flexibility compared to prior attribute-specific fine-tuning methods (MoE, HP+SP), working with any LLM at test time
Summary-level MCTS node design sensibly reduces search complexity while maintaining full summary evaluation
Strong analytical insights through plan diversity analysis (Figure 4), attribute control frequency patterns (Figure 5), and step-wise control visualization (Figure 6)
Well-written paper with clear motivation, effective figures, pseudocode, and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead (8.5x slower than baseline: 196s vs 23s per summary) severely limits practical deployment; justification about faster LMs is insufficient for production systems

No human evaluation despite claims of preserving summary quality; only automatic metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) reported, which don't capture coherence, consistency, or fluency degradation from iterative refinement

Evaluation uses reference summary attributes rather than arbitrary user preferences, making the experimental setup somewhat artificial and not validating whether users want targets matching reference values

Limited algorithmic novelty: applies existing MCTS techniques (PUCT, local rewards) to a new domain rather than developing fundamentally new methods; heuristic value function provides minimal benefit (ablation shows <0.5% improvement)
Self-planning baselines perform unexpectedly poorly, raising questions about prompt engineering quality; comparison feels somewhat unfair given the structured search vs. prompting difference

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or clarification on number of runs; some improvements appear marginal (e.g., topic scores often very similar to baselines)

Limited scope of attributes (only 5 linguistic/structural; no semantic or content-based attributes; speaker only for dialogues); unclear scalability with many attributes; attribute definitions are crude (entity ratio for specificity, embedding similarity for topic)
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices lacking justification: tree depth d=5, 8 simulations, α=1, β=10; non-trivial sensitivity to β shown in Table 5; no systematic ablation on key hyperparameters
Evaluation methodology limitation: uses reference summary attributes as ground truth, but doesn't validate reference quality or investigate user preferences beyond this assumption
Reproducibility concerns: no code/data release mentioned, complex system requires careful implementation, and several design choices lack sufficient justification
